newsitem.title: UK: Snoring dangers exaggerated, researchers say.
newsitem.headline: Snoring dangers exaggerated, researchers say.

text.p: Snoring may make sufferers sleepy and grumpy, but it is probably not a great danger to their health, British researchers concluded on Friday.

In a report sure to anger tired wives seeking to frighten snoring husbands into doing something about their problem, John Wright and colleagues at Bradford Royal Infirmary said they could find no strong links between snoring and disease.

Several studies have linked snoring with problems ranging from heart attacks to car crashes. The big target has been sleep apnoea, a condition that causes sufferers to stop breathing during sleep when their airways close up.

Wright's group reviewed 54 studies in several languages that investigated the possible association between snoring and death, high blood pressure, heartbeat irregularities, stroke, quality of life and road accidents.

"Most were poorly designed and only weak or contradictory evidence was found of an association with cardiac arrhythmias, ischaemic heart disease, cardiac failure...hypertension and stroke," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.

"This systematic review indicates that the evidence for a causal assocation between sleep apnoea and a range of poor health outcomes is generally weak, with the exception of daytime sleepiness and possibly vehicle accidents."
But other experts said snoring was still a possible threat to health and needed to be studied more.

Robert Priest and colleagues at St Mary's Hospital in London and colleagues at California's Stanford University and Montreal's Philippe Pinel Research Centre said snoring disorders were widely under-diagnosed in Britain.
They interviewed 2,800 women and 2,000 men across Britain by telephone.
"Forty percent of the population reported snoring regularly and 3.8 percent reported breathing pauses during sleep," they wrote in a second report in the journal.

"Regular snoring was significantly associated with male sex, age 25 or more, obesity, daytime sleepiness or naps, night-time awakenings, large amounts of caffeine and smoking." Snorers also reported drowsiness while driving.

"Sleep disordered breathing is common and has important implications for the population's health," John Fleetham, a respiratory specialist at Vancouver Hospital in Canada, wrote in a commentary on the findings.

"More studies are needed on the link between sleep disordered breathing and road traffic accidents, taking into account the potential confounding factors of shift work, alcohol and drug use and annual distance covered."
